gen-dafont-disorder-gf-pt-sans-caption: PT Sans Caption has big-bodied lowercase and bowls left invitingly unclosed, which gives this sans-serif a contemporary, easygoing voice. Disorder brings raw, uniform-bar chaos up top while PT Sans Caption stays steady.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-puritan: Puritan is a rounded sans-serif with oversized counters in its e and a, forms staying open to the side. Puritan feels approachable and clean next to the raw, monoline chaos of Disorder.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-questrial: Raw chaos meets stencil-flat tidiness, with Disorder setting its big lowercase well apart and without swelling at the joins. Questrial does the quiet work, open-curved and single-weight, where Disorder does the loud.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-radio-canada: Raw is the right word for Disorder, with its high x-height, wide-set glyphs and no swelling at the curves. But Disorder earns its keep big and short, while Radio Canada, a plain sans, holds the steady line.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-radio-canada-big: Loud letters, tidy partner: Disorder spaces its big lowercase wide while Radio Canada Big keeps terminals clear of the stem. And what ties them is a shared uniform stroke, one shouting while the other speaks plainly.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-readex-pro: Wild up top, level-headed below: Disorder scatters big lowercase glyphs apart while Readex Pro, a sans, keeps broad gaps at every terminal. Paragraphs would read smoothly, the weight never lurching from word to word.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-roboto: Flat stripes of ink against generous round mouths: Disorder keeps every stroke constant, and Roboto, a plain sans, opens its rounds wide. Their sharpest quality is attitude: raw on one side, clean on the other.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-ruda: Raw scatter meets wire-fine tidiness. Disorder sets its big, widely spaced lowercase against Ruda, a sans-serif with a sizable x-height for screens and wide-mouthed rounds, so the page feels friendly.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-saira: No stress axis tilts the round letters of Disorder, which sit well apart with a high x-height. But Saira, a plain sans, does the tidy work, with visible gaps in its s and rounds reaching high.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-sarpanch: Blunt strokes, with no contrast anywhere. Disorder keeps every stem and terminal uniform while Sarpanch, a sans-serif with a clearly open lowercase e and compact ascenders, adds an approachable, contemporary footing.
